Aldehyde. An organic compound containing a carbonyl functional group where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom. Represented as CHO, aldehydes are positioned at the terminal end of a carbon chain, making them highly reactive intermediates that are easily oxidized to carboxylic acids or reduced to primary alcohols.

Aldehydes can be detected qualitatively using Tollens reagent in the silver mirror test. The aldehyde gets oxidized to a carboxylate while reducing diamminesilver ions to metallic silver, creating a characteristic mirror-like coating. They can also be detected using Fehling's solution, which oxidizes the aldehyde and precipitates copper ions as a red copper oxide precipitate.

Aldehydes are typically prepared by mild oxidation of primary alcohols using reagents like pyridinium chlorochromate, or PCC, or through the Swern oxidation. These methods avoid further oxidation to carboxylic acids. They can also be synthesized via ozonolysis of alkenes containing terminal or monosubstituted double bonds, followed by a reductive workup.

Formaldehyde, or methanal, is the simplest aldehyde. It's widely used in aqueous solution as formalin, both as a biological preservative and as a disinfectant. Primary alcohols can be oxidized to aldehydes and then reduced back using sodium borohydride. Strong oxidizing agents like chromic acid will oxidize aldehydes all the way to carboxylic acids. When they share the same molecular formula, aldehydes and ketones are constitutional isomers. Fehling's test uses copper sulfate to distinguish aldehydes from ketones, a key difference between these two functional groups.
